story.title: A town built around the road, the river and the inn
paras: For centuries, Boroughbridge was much more than a Yorkshire market town. Its position on the Great North Road made it an important stopping point for coaches, travellers and horses moving between northern and southern England.
The River Ure brought additional trade, while cattle drovers, horse dealers and visitors to local fairs all contributed to the town’s busy streets.
At its peak, Boroughbridge supported 22 inns. The Crown alone could stable around 100 horses, illustrating the scale of the coaching trade.
During the busy droving season, as many as 2,000 cattle a day crossed the bridge on their way from Scotland to southern markets.
Then the railways changed the town. By 1853, stagecoach transport had disappeared and seven of the original 22 inns had already been lost.
Some former inns became shops or homes. Others disappeared altogether. Several survived and continued to welcome customers.
Today, traces of this history remain hidden in old buildings, street names and the stories of local families.
This archive aims to recover those stories, one pub at a time.

timeline.t: Parliament authorises six locks to make the River Ure navigable as far as Ripon.
Baines's directory lists the Blue Bell and White Horse at Kirby Hill, and the Fox & Hounds and Red Lion at Langthorpe.
The River Ure Navigation, insolvent, is sold to the Leeds and Thirsk Railway Company.
The railway arrives, with a station on the Milby road. (Wikipedia gives 17 June 1847 for the first station.)
Stagecoach transport has disappeared, and seven of the town's 22 inns have been lost.
A second station opens on 1 April.
Bulmer's directory lists the Anchor, Fox and Hounds, Old Red Lion, Grantham Arms, Blue Bell, and the Ship Inn and Railway Tavern beerhouses.
Around this year the Three Horse Shoes is rebuilt as a roadhouse for the Great North Road.
The A1 bridge over the Ure collapses; the army puts up a Bailey bridge.
Passenger trains stop calling at Boroughbridge on 25 September.
The Great North Road is moved west to become the A1. (The town council's history gives 1963 for the bypass.)
Eight pubs or hotels are still trading in the town.
Bernard Porter compiles Hostelries in Boroughbridge, recording 36 sites and what their buildings were then used for.
The Malt Shovel closes permanently on 1 January, according to CAMRA.
The Wild Swan at Minskip closes suddenly in January. In October the Tap on the Tutt closes for refurbishment.

trails.name: Bridge Street and the River Ure
trails.walk: Start by the Ure at the Borough Bridge. The Three Horse Shoes and Riverside Court (once the Blinking Owl) face each other on Bridge Street. Walk south up Bridge Street to the Crown at the junction with Horsefair and Fishergate.

trails.name: Horsefair and St James Square
trails.walk: From the Crown, the old post office building next door on Horsefair is the listed former annexe of the Three Greyhounds Hotel. Return to the Crown and follow Fishergate and the High Street south to St James Square for the Black Bull.

trails.name: High Street and the coaching inns
trails.walk: The Crown and the Black Bull bookend the High Street. The Black Horse, Black Swan, Saddle and White Hart all stood on this street, but their exact buildings are not yet confirmed, so they are not marked. Look up as you walk.

trails.name: Langthorpe and Milby
trails.walk: Cross the Borough Bridge north. The Grantham Arms is on the Milby side; the Anchor stands on Leeming Lane; and the Fox and Hounds is west along Skelton Road. The Langthorpe Loop guide from the town council covers the brewery buildings in more detail.

trails.name: Kirby Hill and the old Great North Road
trails.walk: The Blue Bell stands on Leeming Lane, the old Great North Road, north of Langthorpe. The listed milestone is about 10 metres south of the pub.

milestone.name: Great North Road milestone
milestone.note: Listed early 19th-century milestone, about 10 metres south of the Blue Bell.

pubs.name: Three Horse Shoes
pubs.intro: A former Great North Road pub, notable for its surviving 1930s interior.

history.t: This former Great North Road pub is especially notable for its surviving 1930s interior, retaining original features including wood panelling, a fireplace and unusual shutters above its bar counters. CAMRA recognises the interior as being of outstanding national historic importance.

Historic England dates the present building to about 1930, designed by Sydney Blenkhorn of Knaresborough for Hepworth & Co., brewers of Ripon. It was listed Grade II in 2001 as an increasingly rare inter-war pub interior.

Bernard Porter's family memories name Samuel Morrel (1822) and John Morrel (1828) among its 19th-century landlords, and recall that the army took over the back half of the hotel for about four years during the Second World War.
The premises later traded as the Tap on the Tutt.

status.text: Temporarily closed for refurbishment from 18 October 2026, expected to reopen on or before 24 November 2026.

questions: When did the name change to Tap on the Tutt?
What did the pub look like before the 1930 rebuild?

pubs.name: Crown Hotel
pubs.intro: One of Boroughbridge’s most important coaching inns.

history.t: One of Boroughbridge’s most important coaching inns. The Crown’s stables once accommodated around 100 horses, showing how essential the town was to travellers on the Great North Road.

Coaches through Boroughbridge connected places including Leeds, Newcastle, Durham and Sunderland. The town council's history names the North Star (for Carlisle and Edinburgh), the Defence (for Durham) and the Royal Charlotte (for Sunderland).

Historic England records the site as the former manor house of the Tancred family, with a stone gable surviving on the Fishergate side, and describes the building as an important coaching inn in the later 18th century. It was listed Grade II in 1952.

status.text: Trading as a hotel, restaurant and bar.

questions: Which coaches called at the Crown, rather than elsewhere in the town?
The Crown Hotel's own published history has not yet been reviewed for this archive.

pubs.name: Blinking Owl
pubs.intro: A former hostelry on Bridge Street, facing the Three Horse Shoes across the road.

history.t: Recorded among the historic hostelries of Bridge Street. Bernard Porter's 2010 notes identify the former premises as a care home, showing how former hospitality buildings took on new uses as coaching and local trade changed.
His memories add that it stood opposite the Three Horse Shoes, overlooking the river, and was a licensed restaurant in 1985.
Historic England's listing for Riverside Court, Bridge Street, says it was formerly listed as The Blinking Owl Public House: an early-to-mid 19th-century former pub.

status.text: Former inn. A care home in 2010; present use not yet re-checked.

questions: Is this the inn by the bridge, once a warehouse, that the town council says became homes for the elderly?

pubs.name: Three Greyhounds
pubs.address: Horsefair, beside the old post office, Boroughbridge
pubs.intro: Named for the three greyhounds of the Mauleverer family crest.

history.t: The Three Greyhounds is associated with the Mauleverer family, whose crest featured three greyhounds. The town council's history records the Three Greyhounds building beside the old post office on Horsefair, once the Mauleverer family home, as converted into flats and still carrying the greyhounds of the crest.
The building next door, the Post Office and former annexe to the Three Greyhounds Hotel, is listed Grade II and has an early 19th-century appearance.
Bernard Porter's list also associates the Three Greyhounds name with the Musketeer. The Musketeer was among the eight pubs and hotels the town council recorded as trading in 2005.

pubs.note: These accounts still need reconciling. We have not assumed that the converted flats and the Musketeer were one continuously identifiable pub site.

status.text: The Three Greyhounds building is now flats. The Musketeer was trading in 2005 and later closed, according to pub-directory records.

loc.basis: The pin marks the listed former annexe (the old post office). The council's history places the Greyhounds next to it.

questions: Were the Three Greyhounds and the Musketeer the same building?
When did the hotel stop trading?

pubs.name: New Inn
pubs.address: Horsefair, near the pedestrian crossing, Boroughbridge
pubs.intro: One site, four names.

history.t: This site is notable for the succession of names recorded in the historical compilation: New Inn, Copper Kettle, LJ’s and Farndale Town House. The changes reflect the evolving commercial character of the town centre.
A "Farndale House" was among the eight pubs and hotels trading in the town in 2005.

status.text: Historic hospitality premises. Present use needs verifying.

Is the 2005 Farndale House the same as Farndale Town House?
What is the building used for now?

pubs.name: Black Bull Inn
pubs.intro: An old market-town inn in the corner of St James Square.

history.t: The Black Bull keeps the character of an old market-town inn, with intimate drinking rooms and open fires. CAMRA describes it as a Grade II-listed 13th-century building.

Historic England's listing, made in 1984, gives the building a probable 17th-century origin, much altered in the 18th century and later, with a chamfered ceiling beam and fireplace beam inside. The two dates do not agree, and we have not yet seen evidence for the earlier one.

status.text: Trading inn with rooms.

questions: Is there documentary evidence for a medieval building on the site?
Earliest record of the Black Bull as an inn.

pubs.name: Malt Shovel
pubs.address: St James Square / York Road, Boroughbridge
pubs.intro: A St James Square pub that lasted into the 21st century.

history.t: Known historically as the Malt Shovel, with the Yorkshire Rose also recorded as an earlier name. The Malt Shovel survived into the 21st century and was among Boroughbridge's trading pubs in 2005.
CAMRA records its permanent closure from 1 January 2011, with the premises later used as a shop.

pubs.note: Historic England lists an early 18th-century former pub on Church Lane, near St James Square, as "formerly listed as Yorkshire Rose Public House" (now Stonefield House). It may be this building, but that is not yet confirmed, so no pin is shown.

status.text: Closed permanently on 1 January 2011, according to CAMRA.

questions: Is the listed former Yorkshire Rose on Church Lane the same building?
When did the Yorkshire Rose become the Malt Shovel?

pubs.name: Windmill
pubs.intro: A former hostelry in St James Square.

history.t: The Windmill was a former hostelry in St James Square. Bernard Porter's 2010 account identifies the premises as having become a business called the Dining Room.
His memories add that the Druids met at the Windmill.

status.text: Former pub. Present building use not yet verified.

pubs.name: Three Arrows
pubs.intro: A building that passed between private and hospitality use.

history.t: The town council's historical overview gives the building's origins as a private house called Arrowfield. It later became the Three Arrows and then the Rose Manor, which was trading as a hotel in 2005.
The 2010 compilation describes it as a nursing home.

status.text: Former inn and hotel. A nursing home in 2010; present use needs verifying.

questions: When did Arrowfield become the Three Arrows?
When did the Rose Manor close?

history.t: A former hostelry identified in the historical list with Griffin House. The area lies across the River Tutt from Horsefair and formed part of the historic town's network of streets and squares.

pubs.name: Queen’s Head
pubs.address: Hall Square (also called Butter Tub Square), Boroughbridge
pubs.intro: A former inn in one of the oldest parts of Boroughbridge.

history.t: The Queen’s Head was a former inn in this old part of Boroughbridge. Bernard Porter's 2010 compilation records that the building had become a private house.
His memories add that the Foresters met at the Queen’s Head by Hall Square.

status.text: Former pub. A private house in 2010.

pubs.name: Anchor Inn
pubs.intro: The flagship inn of the old Anchor Brewery.

history.t: A surviving village pub closely tied to the area's brewing history. The Langthorpe Loop guide calls the Anchor the flagship inn of the old Anchor Brewery, whose brewery and maltings buildings are now converted to housing.
Bulmer's 1890 directory lists William Stevenson, tailor and victualler, at the Anchor Inn.
Bernard Porter's memories give its earlier names: the Free Masons, which became the Oddfellows, then the Steam Mill, which later became the Anchor.

status.text: Trading pub.

questions: When did each change of name happen?

pubs.name: Fox and Hounds
pubs.intro: A longstanding Langthorpe pub.

history.t: Bulmer's 1890 directory lists Welbury Watson as victualler at the Fox and Hounds Inn, showing the pub was trading in the late Victorian period.
A Fox & Hounds at Langthorpe also appears in Baines's 1823 directory, kept by Richard Farmery.
The pub remains a familiar part of Langthorpe's hospitality history.

status.text: Trading pub.

questions: Has the pub always been in the present building?

pubs.name: Railway Tavern
pubs.intro: A former beerhouse linked by name and place with the railway.

history.t: A former beerhouse associated by name and location with the railway area. Bulmer's 1890 directory lists Miss Emma Shaw running the Railway Tavern as a beerhouse.
The railway reached the area in 1848 and the line closed in the 1960s. We have found no evidence that the railway caused the tavern to open or close.

status.text: Former beerhouse. The building and closing date need investigating.

questions: When did it open and close?

pubs.name: Old Red Lion
pubs.address: Langthorpe, near the Fox and Hounds
pubs.intro: A Langthorpe inn, now believed to be cottages.

history.t: The Old Red Lion appears in Bulmer's 1890 directory, with Mrs Eliza Whytell as victualler. Bernard Porter's 2010 notes place its former premises among cottages just beyond the Fox and Hounds.
Baines's 1823 directory lists a Red Lion at Langthorpe kept by John Wincup. It may be the same house, but that is not confirmed.

status.text: Former inn, believed to survive as cottages in 2010.

dates.what: Red Lion, John Wincup (possibly the same house)

questions: Was the 1823 Red Lion the same house?

pubs.name: Ship Inn
pubs.address: Langthorpe, first right after crossing the Boroughbridge bridge
pubs.intro: A Langthorpe beerhouse; not the Ship Inn at Aldborough.

history.t: A former Langthorpe beerhouse. Bulmer's 1890 directory lists William Kay at the Ship Inn, as a beerhouse. The 2010 compilation gives its later building as Guisley House.
This is a different establishment from the Ship Inn in Aldborough.

status.text: Former pub. The building was Guisley House in 2010.

pubs.name: Four Alls
pubs.intro: A lost inn whose name came from an old rhyme.

history.t: The Four Alls was one of the former hostelries of the Langthorpe area. Bernard Porter's compilation records that its premises were a private house by 2010.
His memories place it in Milby and quote the verse behind the name: "King — I rule for All. Priest — I pray for All. Soldier — I fight for All. Everyman — I pay for All."

status.text: Former pub, a private house in 2010. Location not confirmed.

questions: Is it connected with Four Alls Farm on Tinkler Lane in Milby?

pubs.name: Grantham Arms
pubs.intro: A surviving inn and hotel on the northern side of Boroughbridge.

history.t: A surviving inn and hotel on the northern side of Boroughbridge. Bernard Porter's list puts the Grantham Arms under Langthorpe, while its present address uses Milby.
Bulmer's 1890 directory lists William Alfred Lister as victualler at the Grantham Arms, Milby. Bernard Porter's memories say it was named after Lord Grantham of Newby Hall.

status.text: Trading pub and hotel.

pubs.name: Ship Inn
pubs.intro: A longstanding village inn close to Roman Aldborough.

history.t: A longstanding village inn in historic Aldborough, close to the remains of the Roman town of Isurium Brigantum. The town council's overview names the Ship among the pubs trading in 2005, and it is still listed by CAMRA.
Historic England lists the building at Grade II as a probable late 16th-century public house.

status.text: Trading pub.

questions: Earliest record of the Ship as an inn.

pubs.name: Crown Inn
pubs.intro: A surviving village inn in a 16th-century building.

pubs.name: White Swan
pubs.intro: A village inn that grew into a dining pub.

history.t: This traditional village pub was known as the White Swan and later traded as the Wild Swan. It grew from a small village inn into a larger dining pub.
The White Swan (Minskip) was among the pubs near the town still trading in 2005.
The Stray Ferret reported on 8 January 2026 that the Wild Swan had closed suddenly, with its future uncertain.

status.text: Closed since January 2026; future uncertain.

questions: When did the White Swan become the Wild Swan?

pubs.name: Blue Bell Inn
pubs.intro: An old coaching inn on the road between London and Scotland.

history.t: The Langthorpe Loop guide calls the Blue Bell an old coaching inn that still has a cell in its grounds, where prisoners bound for York could be chained up overnight.
The guide also points out the nearby milestone, which it says marks the spot exactly halfway between the Scottish and English capitals. The milestone is listed by Historic England.
Baines's 1823 directory lists Grace Pickering, common brewer, maltster and victualler, at the Blue Bell. Bulmer's 1890 directory lists Francis Kirk, victualler and farmer.

status.text: Trading pub with rooms.

questions: How old is the prisoners' cell?

pubs.name: White Horse
pubs.intro: A former Kirby Hill hostelry known by two names.

history.t: Bernard Porter's compilation identifies this former hostelry under the names White Horse and White Swan. The dates of the different names and the original location need further investigation.
Baines's 1823 directory lists Matthew Hanby, victualler, at the White Horse, Kirby Hill.

status.text: Former inn. Exact site not verified.

pubs.name: Wellesley Arms
pubs.intro: Demolished to make way for the A1(M).

history.t: A former Kirby Hill hostelry named after Sir J. R. A. Wellesley, identified in the historical compilation as Lord of the Manor of Kirby Hill.
The 2010 account says the inn was eventually demolished to make way for what is now the A1(M).

status.text: Demolished for the A1(M).

questions: Where exactly did it stand? A comparison of maps from before and after the A1(M) could show this.

history.t: A surviving social club recorded by CAMRA. Its opening date and earlier history need further research.
